criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: Count and quality are not the problem: seven peer-reviewed studies (Bertram et al. 2010, Ko et al. 2007, Pascarella et al. 2018, Dourish & Bellotti 1992, Whitson 2018, Stray et al. 2016, Maddila et al. 2023) clear the HD requirement for six including academic research articles, and every entry avoids my pet peeve - each says what specifically was learnt (21 information types across seven kinds of work; 61% unsatisfied; 80% vs 30% Development-category files; 86 of 119 rejected alerts) and how it is used. Three things hold it off HD. (1) The synthesis contradicts its own frame. The review opens by promising three explanations - 'The literature offers three explanations: reporting is structured against the reporter (Dourish & Bellotti, 1992), the tools hide what happened (Whitson, 2018), or the report is addressed to the wrong audience (Stray et al., 2016)' - but the closing paragraph 'The six do three jobs' silently drops Stray from the accounting, and the adjudication sentence 'The project bets on the structural mechanism; if readers can say what changed but not why, opacity wins' assigns an outcome to two mechanisms and none to the third. A mechanism introduced, sourced and then dropped is not expert synthesis; it is a loose end I will notice. (2) Washburn et al. (2016) arrives only as a drive-by inside the synthesis - 'found no communication category among 155 game postmortems' - with no summary, no evaluation and no method, so it reads as a source added for count rather than used. (3) The synthesis is telegraphic rather than expert: 'The six do three jobs. Bertram shows the record failing and Maddila sets the bar a fix must clear.' That is a table of allocations written as prose; it abstracts, but it does not explain the relationships to a reader who has not been living in the corpus. Two sentences also fail on their own terms: 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it' has no antecedent, because Bertram's remedy is never stated; and 'Their own example is the version-control edit log, today's commit message' compresses a 1992 finding, a 2026 equivalence and a corpus example into one clause.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Rewrite the closing synthesis paragraph so all three named mechanisms are adjudicated. Name Stray's audience mechanism in 'The six do three jobs' (make it seven and say so), give it a predicted outcome alongside the structural and opacity bets, and state Bertram's rejected remedy explicitly in his entry so 'That remedy' has an antecedent. Pay for the ~35 words by cutting the Washburn sentence entirely (it is doing no work the rest of the paragraph does not already do) and by shortening 'Their evidence is narrow: four groups, one session, in 1992, but the mechanism is about incentives, not technology' to 'Their evidence is narrow - four groups in one 1992 session - but the mechanism is about incentives, not technology.'

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: Much of this is HD-shaped. Four goals span understand to create, are phrased as capabilities, each carries a Measure, and 'Evaluate: judge whether a team's artefacts can serve a producer's information need, or whether a person must' is exactly the level I said I expect. The research question is genuinely insightful. The methodology is properly mixed - counterbalanced matched comprehension items scored at Endsley's three levels, plus think-alouds coded against Ko's 21 types with a re-coding agreement check. The scoping evidence is well past 'the hello world of that tool': a real Editor package running on a real SS3D week (Figure 2), the serialisation argument evidenced in Figure 3, a measured 46-100% naming presence across four weeks, and a BuildReport probe. Hours sum to 65 with 15 in prac, and the Kickstarter tiering with a stated overrun order ('An overrun consumes the challenge tier first, then the stretch tier') is exactly what I asked for. What keeps it at D is that the pieces do not fully fit together, which is one of the five things a proposal has to convince me of. (1) Deliverable 1 is a 12-hour second study - heuristic evaluation of four tools, 10 job ads, 15 reviews, two interviews, 25 classified needs - and almost none of it reappears in the evaluation design. The Scoping Evidence section runs on SS3D and eight readers; the tool-UX study is a bolt-on whose output touches the study only through a needs list. (2) That join is where the one hard inconsistency sits: 'All eight readers then classify the same ten needs at the end of their session' - ten, where Deliverable 1 produced 25, with no statement of how the ten are chosen, which is exactly the kind of selection a reader will suspect was made after seeing the data. (3) The corpus paragraph reads as self-contradiction: 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough, nor does my own team's' followed immediately by 'the Unity Experiment Framework, the best-linked repository, serves Sub-question 1' - UXF failed the 30-per-100 threshold at 20, so the proposal needs one sentence saying why 20 suffices for a derivability analysis when it did not suffice for the reader study. (4) 'The 60% target sits above the worst week' is a defence that concedes the point: a success measure set above your worst observed value (46%) is one the committed tier can miss on a bad week, and there is no stated response if it does.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Close the join between Deliverable 1 and the study. Replace 'All eight readers then classify the same ten needs at the end of their session' with a sentence that states the selection rule in advance and fixes it before data collection, e.g. 'From the 25 classified needs I pre-select ten before recruitment - the five I mark derivable and the five I mark not derivable that were raised most often in Deliverable 1 - and all eight readers classify that fixed set at the end of their session.' Add a half-sentence justifying UXF for Sub-question 1 ('its 20 links per 100 commits are enough to trace needs to artefacts, though not enough to build a week's report from'). Pay for both by cutting 'Briefed proxies stand in for studio producers, a limit I report' (the limitation is already implied by 'student producers') and by compressing Deliverable 1's success-measure cell.

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Structure, figures and referencing are strong: three relevant, well-captioned images all cited in the body, correct section headings, APA references with no orphans in either direction, 2,461 body words, appendices that carry the bulk without being load-bearing. There are essentially no spelling or grammatical errors. What stops it at CR is density, and this is the same student whose A1 came back with 'So much information in each slide... You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context.' The prose has been compressed to fit the ceiling until sentences carry two or three facts each with the connectives removed, and I had to read the following twice: 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it: my evaluation scores each report against the team's history, not its tickets.'; 'The six do three jobs.'; 'Week difficulty is then a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.'; 'Across four SS3D weeks, between 46% and 100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text (23 of 26 in the week shown). The 60% target sits above the worst week.'; 'It can falsify naming and activity claims, not file counts.'; 'Games are harder: most of their files are not code'; 'The prototype classifies files only; the committed tier (the version I commit to delivering) adds object naming (Figure 3), with the AssetDatabase resolving identifiers to asset and script names.'; 'Deliverable 1 runs across the break and Week 9; the committed tier and instruments land in Week 10; the fidelity check, tier freeze and pilot in Week 11; sessions in Week 12; analysis and video in Week 13.' That last one is a whole schedule delivered as one semicolon chain. The colon-then-clipped-list construction ('Its limits: every signal comes from inside the pull request...') recurs often enough to read as a house style rather than emphasis, and the Scoping Evidence section throws the reader from SS3D statistics to package internals to recruitment to scoring without a paragraph that says plainly what a session looks like from the participant's side. D asks for 'very easy to read'; this is readable but effortful, and torn between CR and D I report CR because the one real marker who has read this student's work made exactly this complaint.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Spend 60-80 words buying air in Scoping Evidence: open the section with two plain sentences that describe one session end to end before any numbers ('A session works like this: a student producer reads a one-page report for a week of a real Unity project, answers six questions about it, then reads a second report for a different week and answers six more. Half see the version that names the changed scenes and prefabs first.'), and break the Week 9-13 semicolon chain into two sentences. Pay for it by cutting 'Briefed proxies stand in for studio producers, a limit I report' and by shortening the Figure 1 caption, which restates Appendix A.

top_changes.location: The six do three jobs. Bertram shows the record failing and Maddila sets the bar a fix must clear.
top_changes.problem: The synthesis contradicts the review's own opening frame. Three mechanisms are promised (structural, opacity, audience - Dourish & Bellotti, Whitson, Stray); the synthesis accounts for six sources and drops Stray, and the closing bet gives an outcome to only two of the three. This is the single most visible defect in the highest-weighted criterion, because it is the paragraph a marker reads to decide whether the review synthesises or merely lists.
top_changes.fix: Rewrite as: 'The seven do three jobs. Bertram shows the record failing and Maddila sets the bar a fix must clear. Dourish and Bellotti, Whitson and Stray explain why - by incentive, by opacity, by audience. Pascarella and Ko describe what a game week and a reader's needs contain. Each explanation predicts a different result: if passive extraction repairs the record, the structural account holds; if readers can say what changed but not why, opacity wins; if they can say both but still ask who the report is for, the audience account does.' Pay for it by deleting the Washburn sentence ('Washburn et al. (2016) found no communication category... one more reason to look in artefacts'), which is an unsummarised drive-by.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review 79 to 82-84; closes the gap to HD on 'expertly synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships'.

top_changes.location: All eight readers then classify the same ten needs at the end of their session;
top_changes.problem: Unexplained number. Deliverable 1 classifies 25 needs; the study uses ten, with no selection rule. A marker reads an unstated selection as a post-hoc one, which undermines the quantitative arm of Sub-question 1.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: 'From the 25 classified needs I pre-select ten before recruitment - the five I mark derivable and the five I mark not derivable that Deliverable 1 saw raised most often - and all eight readers classify that fixed set at the end of their session.' Pay for the extra words by cutting 'Briefed proxies stand in for studio producers, a limit I report.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal 80 to 82; removes the clearest unsupported number in the methodology.

marker_malcolm.notes: SENTENCES THAT NEEDED A SECOND READ (density is this student's documented failure mode; the real A1 marker wrote 'So much information in each slide... You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context'): (1) 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it: my evaluation scores each report against the team's history, not its tickets.' - no antecedent for 'That remedy'. (2) 'The six do three jobs.' - telegraphic, and the count is wrong against the seven studies reviewed. (3) 'Their own example is the version-control edit log, today's commit message; in my corpus, "Fix restart bug (#588)" names an intention while touching 35 files across five categories.' - three moves in one sentence. (4) 'Games are harder: most of their files are not code' - harder than what. (5) 'The prototype classifies files only; the committed tier (the version I commit to delivering) adds object naming (Figure 3), with the AssetDatabase resolving identifiers to asset and script names.' - a definition parenthesis inside a technical clause. (6) 'Across four SS3D weeks, between 46% and 100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text (23 of 26 in the week shown). The 60% target sits above the worst week.' (7) 'Week difficulty is then a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.' (8) 'It can falsify naming and activity claims, not file counts.' (9) 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough, nor does my own team's: its sprint pages were written up after the fact for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A).' (10) 'Deliverable 1 runs across the break and Week 9; the committed tier and instruments land in Week 10; the fidelity check, tier freeze and pilot in Week 11; sessions in Week 12; analysis and video in Week 13.' The recurring construction is colon-then-clipped-list, which appears at least six times and reads as a house style rather than emphasis. CONTRADICTIONS AND UNSUPPORTED NUMBERS: (a) three mechanisms promised in the Literature Review's opening, only two adjudicated in its close, and Stray dropped from 'The six do three jobs'; (b) seven studies reviewed, called 'the six'; (c) ten needs classified by readers vs 25 classified in Deliverable 1, with no selection rule; (d) UXF declared to fail the linkage threshold (20 per 100 against a stated 30 per 100) and then used for Sub-question 1 without justification; (e) SS3D appears as 17.5% in Figure 1 and 24% in Figure 2 and Appendix C - reconciled only in Appendix A, which the marker may not read; (f) the 90%-supported fidelity threshold and the 60% naming target are both asserted without derivation; (g) Washburn et al. (2016) is cited for an absence ('no communication category among 155 game postmortems') without being summarised or evaluated anywhere. MECHANICAL-TRAP CHECK: Topic Category present on the cover ('Developer / production tools') - yes. Student ID is the placeholder '[STUDENT ID]' - must be filled. A bracketed '[CONFIRM BEFORE SUBMISSION...]' line sits immediately after the Generative AI statement - must be deleted; both are on the student's own list and I marked the document as if filled. No residual template instruction text found in the body. Word count: 2,461 body plus 27 cover, under the 2,500 limit excluding references - compliant, and the appendices correctly carry non-vital material. Hours: 12+16+4+3+15+7+4+2+2 = 65, and the in-prac column 2+5+1+1+4+1+1+0+0 = 15 - both correct, and the tier hours (committed 11 + stretch 3 + challenge 2 = 16) reconcile with Deliverable 2's 16. Figures: three, numbered 1-3, each captioned and each cited in the body text; all three carry information rather than decoration, which is what I want. Generative AI statement: present, specific about what AI did, and names an evidence file (GENAI-EVIDENCE.md) - good, and declaring the five caught AI errors is a strength, not a liability. References: APA, consistent, complete; every in-text citation appears in the list (Anderson & Krathwohl, Bertram, Dourish & Bellotti, Endsley, Ko, Maddila, Nielsen 1994, Nielsen & Molich 1990, Pascarella, Stray, Washburn, Whitson) and every list entry is cited somewhere, the seven vendor and grey sources in Appendix A. Endsley (1995) is correctly given as Human Factors 37(1), 32-64. I could not verify the docx's table-of-contents field state from the source; update fields before upload. BAND DECISIONS: torn between HD and D on both Literature Review and Project Proposal, and I report D on both - on the review because the synthesis drops a mechanism it introduced, on the proposal because Deliverable 1 and the study do not fully join and the ten-needs number is unexplained. Torn between D and CR on Communication, and I report CR, because the one real marker who has assessed this student's work on this project penalised exactly this compression, and nothing in the prose since then has loosened. Predicted task mark 0.45x79 + 0.40x80 + 0.15x73 = 78.5, reported as 78 (D). Note for the student: this is a strong proposal whose remaining risk is not research and not scope - it is that a tired marker at 11pm has to work to read it. The three highest-value hours between now and submission are spent adding air, not adding content.

criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The source count and quality clear HD (seven peer-reviewed entries plus Washburn, all venue-credible, all evaluated rather than abstracted), so the block on HD is not the corpus - it is the synthesis and the readability of the synthesis. HD wants the review to 'expertly synthesise and abstract key patterns'. The closing paragraph does not. It opens 'The six do three jobs' after seven sources have been presented, and the roll-call that follows - 'Bertram shows the record failing and Maddila sets the bar a fix must clear. Dourish and Bellotti, with Whitson, explain why. Pascarella and Ko describe what a game week and a reader's needs contain.' - silently drops Stray, the source the review itself introduced as the third of three explanations ('or the report is addressed to the wrong audience (Stray et al., 2016)'). So the paragraph that is supposed to adjudicate the three mechanisms only adjudicates two: 'The project bets on the structural mechanism; if readers can say what changed but not why, opacity wins.' Audience is never put in the contest, which means one counted source contributes a design constant ('Both report versions are therefore addressed to the producer') and nothing testable. Second block: the synthesis is six sentences of compression doing the work of a paragraph of argument, and the A1 marker has already told this student what that costs. Third, smaller: the Bertram entry's second sentence has a referent failure - 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it' - where no remedy has been stated; the preceding quotation describes bugs not being filed, not a proposed fix. I had to read that twice, and a marker who reads it once will not see the evaluative move the student is making, which is exactly the move that earns marks.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Rewrite the synthesis paragraph so all three named mechanisms are adjudicated and Stray earns his slot. Concretely: replace 'Dourish and Bellotti, with Whitson, explain why.' with 'Dourish and Bellotti, Whitson and Stray each explain why, and they predict different repairs: passive extraction fixes a structural failure, but not one caused by opacity (the page would say what changed, not why) and not one caused by audience (the page would be complete but unread). My comprehension items separate the three: an unanswered what-changed item indicts extraction, an unanswered what-it-means item indicts opacity, and a reader who scores well but says the page is not for them indicts audience.' Pay for it by cutting the Maddila sentence 'Before that check existed, 86 of 119 alerts that developers rejected had fired despite recent activity on the pull request.' down to 'Before that check, most developer-rejected alerts had fired despite recent activity.' That single change converts a list into an abstraction and makes the review predict something.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The scoping evidence is genuinely advanced - a running Unity Editor package shown docked in the Editor on a real 2021 SS3D week (Figure 2), a six-repository measurement the student ran himself (Figure 1), a measured 46-100% naming-presence figure that sets the 60% target above the worst week, and a build-report probe. That is well past 'hello world'. The mixed methodology is real (scored comprehension items at Endsley's three levels plus think-alouds coded against Ko's 21 types with re-coding agreement). What keeps it out of HD is that the headline research question is not the question the study is powered to answer. The proposal asks 'Which of a producer's information needs can be answered automatically from the artefacts a team already produces - and which can't?' but the method for Sub-question 1 is 'Deliverable 1's specification marks each need derivable, partly derivable or not derivable against a named artefact' - that is the student's own judgement - plus eight readers classifying ten needs and reporting agreement. Agreement with my own marking is not evidence that an artefact can or cannot answer a need; it is evidence about how readers guess. Every empirical lever in the design (counterbalancing, matched items, fidelity check, unanswerable item) serves Sub-question 2, the naming manipulation. HD wants 'a highly appropriate and achievable mixed methodology' for the stated question, and here the methodology is appropriate to the sub-question and only partly to the question on the cover. Second reason: recruitment, which is where student studies die. 'The target is eight readers, six of whom also think aloud; the floor is five readers and five think-alouds.' At the floor every reader also thinks aloud, which is a different design - thinking aloud on a stand-up task after the scored items risks contaminating the second report's scores and the floor never says which arm runs first in that case. Third: the hour table balances at exactly 65 with 15 in prac, but Deliverable 1 spends 12 hours on a second, formative study (four tools heuristically evaluated, 10 job ads, 15 reviews, two interviews, 25 needs classified) in the break and Week 9, leaving 16 hours to build both report conditions plus AssetDatabase object naming and land them in Week 10. Malcolm's own line about estimating applies; nothing in the text acknowledges that Deliverable 1 is the most cuttable thing in the plan if the build slips - the overrun policy only sheds the challenge and stretch tiers.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Give Sub-question 1 an evidential arm rather than a judgement arm, in two sentences, and fix the floor. Replace 'All eight readers then classify the same ten needs at the end of their session; I report their agreement with one another and with my marking, and treat each disagreement as a finding about what the artefacts cannot say.' with 'For the ten needs, each reader attempts to answer the need from the report in front of them and rates their confidence; a need is evidenced as derivable when readers answer it correctly from the report, and as not derivable when the report is silent or they answer wrongly with high confidence. My prior classification is recorded before the sessions and scored against that outcome, so disagreements are measured against reader behaviour, not against my opinion.' Then add to the recruitment paragraph: 'At the floor, all five read both reports and think aloud only after the second report is scored.' Pay for both by cutting 'Week difficulty is then a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.' to 'Per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.'

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Structure, figures, referencing and word count are all in order - headings follow the template, three figures are numbered, captioned and cited in the body, every reference is cited somewhere and every in-text citation is in the list, APA is consistent, and the body is 2,461 words. But D requires the report to be 'very easy to read', and it is not. The prose is at maximum compression throughout: almost every sentence carries a number, a mechanism and a design consequence at once, and the connective tissue has been squeezed out to make the ceiling. This is precisely the failure the A1 marker named ('So much information in each slide... You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context'), and it has migrated into the writing. Examples I had to re-read: 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it' (no antecedent for 'That remedy'); 'The prototype classifies files only; the committed tier (the version I commit to delivering) adds object naming (Figure 3), with the AssetDatabase resolving identifiers to asset and script names' (three separate facts, one clause each, plus a parenthetical gloss of the student's own coinage); 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough, nor does my own team's: its sprint pages were written up after the fact for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue' ('written up after the fact for a semester' is not English I can parse on one pass); 'It can falsify naming and activity claims, not file counts' (no subject a reader can hold - 'it' is the fidelity check two sentences back). There is also a visible internal contradiction: 'The six do three jobs' follows seven presented sources, and the Introduction states 'eight student producers read two versions of the report' as settled fact while the Scoping section describes eight as a target with a floor of five. A marker who notices the first will distrust the second. Nothing here is a spelling or grammar error - the writing is clean - it is density, and density is what this marker is now calibrated to punish.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Do one own-voice readability pass whose only goal is to buy two orienting sentences and spend them at the two places a reader lands cold. First, at the head of Scoping Evidence, before 'Two sub-questions structure the evaluation', add: 'The study is simple in shape: eight readers each read two weekly reports built from the same real project, one naming the changed scenes and prefabs and one not, and answer the same six questions about each.' Second, fix the three referent failures named above by naming their subjects ('Bertram's participants' remedy...', 'The fidelity check can falsify...'). Pay for it by cutting 'Their own example is the version-control edit log, today's commit message; in my corpus, "Fix restart bug (#588)" names an intention while touching 35 files across five categories.' to 'Their own example is the version-control edit log - today's commit message, which in my corpus names an intention while touching 35 files.' and by deleting 'Seven existing tools each cover one part of this (Appendix A): they summarise tickets and commits for engineers, take manual entry from game teams, or show asset history to developers and artists.' down to 'Seven existing tools each cover one part of this (Appendix A); none turns the Unity asset layer into a week's account for a producer.'

top_changes.location: Literature Review, final paragraph: "The six do three jobs. Bertram shows the record failing and Maddila sets the bar a fix must clear."
top_changes.problem: The synthesis names six but seven sources have been presented, and it drops Stray - the source introduced as the third of the three explanations. The paragraph therefore fails to adjudicate the mechanism it set up (audience), and one counted source is left contributing only a design constant. This is the single thing standing between the Literature Review and HD, and the count error invites the marker to audit the whole source list.
top_changes.fix: Replace 'Dourish and Bellotti, with Whitson, explain why.' with 'Dourish and Bellotti, Whitson and Stray each explain why, and they predict different repairs: passive extraction fixes a structural failure, but not one caused by opacity (the page says what changed, not why) or by audience (the page is complete but unread). My comprehension items separate them.' Change 'The six do three jobs' to 'The seven do three jobs'. Pay for the added words by shortening the Maddila sentence 'Before that check existed, 86 of 119 alerts that developers rejected had fired despite recent activity on the pull request.' to 'Before that check, most developer-rejected alerts had fired despite recent activity.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review 78 to 82-84; roughly +2 on the task mark, and it is the only realistic route into the HD band on the 45% criterion.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence: "All eight readers then classify the same ten needs at the end of their session; I report their agreement with one another and with my marking..."
top_changes.problem: The primary research question is answered by the student's own classification plus an agreement exercise. Agreement with the author's marking is not evidence about what artefacts can tell a producer; it is evidence about how readers guess. The rubric's HD wants 'a highly appropriate and achievable mixed methodology' for the stated question, and right now the methodology is built for Sub-question 2 only.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: 'For the ten needs, each reader attempts to answer the need from the report in front of them and rates their confidence; a need is evidenced as derivable when readers answer it correctly from the report, and as not derivable when the report is silent or they answer confidently and wrongly. My prior classification is recorded before the sessions and scored against that outcome.' Pay for it by cutting 'Week difficulty is then a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.' to 'Per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal 79 to 82-84; about +1.5 on the task mark, and it removes the most likely live-defence attack ('how does your study actually answer your own research question?').

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence, recruitment paragraph: "The target is eight readers, six of whom also think aloud; the floor is five readers and five think-alouds."
top_changes.problem: At the floor every reader also thinks aloud, which is a different design from the target, and the text never says whether the think-aloud runs before or after the scored items. If a participant thinks aloud on a stand-up task and then reads the second report, the quantitative arm is contaminated by their own verbalised reasoning. Recruitment shortfall is the normal outcome for a student study, so the floor is the design I expect to actually happen - it needs the same care as the target.
top_changes.fix: Add one sentence: 'In every session the scored items for both reports are completed before any think-aloud, so the floor design (five readers who all think aloud) does not contaminate the quantitative arm.' Pay for it by deleting 'A pilot session runs first; its data is excluded.' from its current position and folding it into the Deliverable 3 success measure, which already says 'piloted and revised in Week 11'.
top_changes.mark_impact: Protects Project Proposal from slipping under a strict marker; worth about half a mark, more in the marker's confidence in the feasibility argument.

top_changes.location: Literature Review, Bertram entry: "That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it: my evaluation scores each report against the team's history, not its tickets."
top_changes.problem: 'That remedy' has no antecedent. The preceding sentence is a participant quote about bugs not being filed - a symptom, not a remedy. The evaluative move here (rejecting a path, which I explicitly reward) is invisible on a first read, so the student gets no credit for the best thing in the entry.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: 'Bertram's teams fixed this by asking developers to file more, which still charges the under-reporting party; I do not take that path, so my evaluation scores each report against the team's commit history rather than its tickets.' Cost-neutral.
top_changes.mark_impact: Recovers evaluative credit on one of the six counted sources; supports the Literature Review at the top of D and helps Communication.

top_changes.location: Introduction: "The project delivers that tool and an evaluation in which eight student producers read two versions of the report..."
top_changes.problem: The Introduction states eight participants as a settled fact; Scoping Evidence calls eight a target with a floor of five. A marker reading both sees an overclaim in the section meant to establish trust, and it is the kind of small inconsistency that makes the rest of the numbers feel less audited.
top_changes.fix: Change 'eight student producers' to 'up to eight student producers'. One word, cost-neutral.
top_changes.mark_impact: Removes a credibility ding across Proposal and Communication; small but free.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence and Figure 2: the report shown to producers lists categories "Code, ScenePrefab, Art, Audio, DataConfig, Meta", with Meta at 30 of 104 entries.
top_changes.problem: The whole Stray argument is that a report thins when it is addressed to the wrong audience, and the proposal answers that with 'Both report versions are therefore addressed to the producer.' But the artefact in Figure 2 shows a non-technical producer a 'Meta' row (29% of the week's entries) and a 'DataConfig' row - engine vocabulary that means nothing to the audience the project claims. The evidence in the figure contradicts the design claim in the prose, and a marker who has just read the Stray paragraph will see it.
top_changes.fix: Add one sentence after the Figure 2 paragraph: 'The producer-facing report merges .meta entries into the asset they accompany and renames DataConfig to "settings and data"; Figure 2 shows the developer-facing debug view the extractor exposes.' If that is not true yet, make it a Deliverable 2 success measure instead: 'no engine-internal category appears in the producer-facing report'. Pay for it by cutting 'It can falsify naming and activity claims, not file counts.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Closes the one place where a figure undercuts the argument; worth up to a mark on Project Proposal and it is the question I would ask first in the prac.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence: "No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough, nor does my own team's: its sprint pages were written up after the fact for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A)."
top_changes.problem: Unparseable on one read ('written up after the fact for a semester'), and it buries a genuinely strong finding - that the student went looking for tracker-repository linkage across six repositories including his own team's and found it does not exist, which is why the study reads the asset layer only. Presented this way it reads as an excuse rather than as a scoping result.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: 'None of the six repositories I screened links tickets to commits densely enough to fuse the two: linkage peaked at 20 genuine references per 100 commits, and my own team's 126 commits cite no Jira issue at all (Appendix A). The study therefore reads the asset layer only, and the Unity Experiment Framework, the best-linked repository, serves Sub-question 1.' Pay for it by deleting the existing final clause it replaces.
top_changes.mark_impact: Turns a buried caveat into scoping evidence; supports the 'strongly convincing argument for feasibility' descriptor and helps Communication.

top_changes.location: Deliverables table, row 1: "Production-tool UX study and design spec ... 12 h" and the overrun policy "An overrun consumes the challenge tier first, then the stretch tier."
top_changes.problem: Twelve hours - nearly a fifth of the budget - goes to a second, formative study that runs before the build, while the build itself (both report conditions plus AssetDatabase naming) has 16 hours and must land in Week 10. The overrun policy only sheds the challenge and stretch tiers, which together are five hours; it does not cover the case where Deliverable 1 overruns and eats the build window. Malcolm will ask about the variance at A3 and the proposal currently has no answer prepared.
top_changes.fix: Add one sentence after the overrun policy: 'If Deliverable 1 overruns, its interview and review-coding arms are cut to the heuristic evaluation and the 25-need classification, because only the need classification feeds Sub-question 1; the build window is not reduced.' Pay for it by cutting 'A live tracker connection is out of scope; so is a language-model prose layer, which could not pass the fidelity check.' to 'A live tracker connection and a language-model prose layer are out of scope; neither could pass the fidelity check.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Strengthens feasibility under the Proposal criterion and pre-buys the A3 hour-variance explanation; about half a mark now, more later.

top_changes.location: Learning Goals: "**Apply -> Analyse:** run heuristic evaluation, then reconcile its findings against interviews and reviews. *Measure:* four tools coded, one reconciliation naming three disagreements."
top_changes.problem: This is the only one of the four goals whose measure is a count of outputs rather than a capability the student can demonstrate afterwards - it reads as a deliverable in goal clothing, which is the mistake the unit explicitly warns against. The other three are well framed ('unaided, state each mechanism, its source and a breakdown it predicts' is exactly right).
top_changes.fix: Replace the measure with: 'Given a production tool I have not evaluated, I can run a heuristic pass, predict which findings user reports will corroborate and which they will not, and say why - naming three disagreements from my four-tool pass as evidence.' Cost-neutral.
top_changes.mark_impact: Removes the one soft goal; small, but the rubric's HD wants 'specific and achievable learning goals' and the A1 marker already praised this student's goals - do not hand back that advantage.

top_changes.location: Cover page: "Student ID: [STUDENT ID]" and after the GenAI statement: "[CONFIRM BEFORE SUBMISSION: which of the six counted sources Raphael has read in full]"
top_changes.problem: Two placeholders remain in the document. The second is worse than a blank field because it is a note-to-self visible to the marker that raises the question of whether the six sources were read - the exact question the Literature Review criterion exists to answer.
top_changes.fix: Fill the Student ID. Delete the CONFIRM line entirely and, if anything replaces it, make it a plain sentence in the GenAI statement: 'I read each of the seven cited studies in full and wrote my own summary of each before drafting this review.' Only write that if it is true.
top_changes.mark_impact: Mechanical; leaving them in costs Communication a band on its own and invites suspicion on the Literature Review.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the seven counted studies have actually been read in full, and whether own-words potted summaries exist.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The student showing me his own-words summary of each paper before the prac - one paragraph each, no quotations. The [CONFIRM] placeholder in the document says this is unresolved, and the specificity of the entries (61% of cases, 86 of 119, 75% ownership share) is consistent with either real reading or careful extraction.

evidence_needed.item: Whether eight COMP3151 student producers can actually be booked for 45-minute sessions in Week 12.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Named commitments - a list of people who have said yes, with slots, by end of Week 10 as the proposal itself requires. Week 12 collides with COMP3151's own release deliverable; verbal interest is not a booking.

evidence_needed.item: Whether object naming via AssetDatabase actually works end to end, or only the file classification does.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A run of the committed tier on the second study week showing named prefabs and scenes in the report output. Figure 2 shows classification only; Figure 3 shows that names exist in the YAML, which is not the same as the tool resolving them. The 60% naming target is currently a measurement of the corpus, not of the tool.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the six comprehension items are answerable from the report alone and discriminate between the two conditions.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The pilot. Appendix B's item 5 ('the treatment version names the nine prefabs') is the only item where the manipulation obviously bites; if the other four scored items are answerable equally well from both versions, the quantitative arm cannot move.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the fidelity check's 90% supported threshold has ever been run on a real week.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: One scored week, with the tally. The proposal describes the procedure but reports no result, so 'It passes when none is contradicted and 90% are supported' is a rule with no observation behind it.

evidence_needed.item: Prac attendance and 1-on-1 record from here to Week 13.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Turning up. Engagement at A3 is read from the weekly conversations and the diary; Deliverable 8 budgets two hours for the diary, which only works if it is written weekly rather than assembled in Week 13.

marker_mitchell.notes: SOURCE-BY-SOURCE CARS AND USE VERDICTS. Bertram et al. (2010), CSCW, ACM, peer-reviewed - Credibility pass (Greenberg/Walker, established CSCW group); Accuracy pass (method stated: interviews and survey, 15 people, four teams; quote page-located at p. 296); Reasonableness pass (claim scoped to small collocated teams); Support pass (DOI, venue). What was specifically learnt: stated and concrete - the record fails at the point of entry, with the participant quote as evidence. How used: stated - the evaluation scores against history rather than tickets. Evaluative move present (a rejected remedy) but wrecked by the 'That remedy' referent failure. Ko et al. (2007), ICSE, peer-reviewed - CARS pass on all four; currency old but the taxonomy is the point. Specifically learnt: yes, and the best entry in the review for my criterion - 21 information types across seven kinds of work, 61% unsatisfied for 'What code caused this program state?', plus the inference that the obstacle was the tool because developers went to the debugger not a colleague. Used: coding frame for the think-alouds, and transfer explicitly limited ('The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers'). Strong. Pascarella et al. (2018), MSR, peer-reviewed - CARS pass; sample stated (30 game, 30 non-game). Specifically learnt: 80% vs 30% development-category files, ownership above a 75% contribution share forming around non-code categories only in games. Used: the report categorises by file type. Best evaluative move in the document: the limitation (no Unity or Unreal in the sample) is named and then repaired by the student's own six-repository measurement, Figure 1. This is HD-grade handling of one source. Dourish and Bellotti (1992), CSCW, peer-reviewed - Credibility pass (canonical); Accuracy pass; currency flagged by the student himself; Reasonableness pass. Specifically learnt: the incentive asymmetry and sender-determined relevance and timing. Used: motivates passive extraction. Quality explicitly evaluated ('four groups, one session, in 1992, but the mechanism is about incentives, not technology') - exactly the CARS reasoning I asked for. Whitson (2018), New Media and Society, peer-reviewed journal - CARS pass; interpretive ethnography correctly described as narrow ('Ten interns at one studio make a narrow, interpretive base'), and the site correctly stated as a large studio in Canada rather than over-specified. Specifically learnt: opacity, the voodoo framing, the shark model example, and the social function of blaming the tool. Used: as a falsifiable hypothesis about what the report will and will not explain. Good. Stray et al. (2016), Journal of Systems and Software, peer-reviewed - CARS pass; grounded theory, 12 teams, three companies, nine interviewees reporting tune-out. Specifically learnt: yes, the audience-shift mechanism. Used: weakly - 'Both report versions are therefore addressed to the producer' makes it a constant, not a variable, and the synthesis then omits it entirely. This is the one counted source whose usefulness to the project is not demonstrated. Maddila et al. (2023), TOSEM - CARS pass (industrial deployment, top journal). Specifically learnt: very precise - the activity gate, the 24-hour window, 86 of 119 rejected alerts. Used: sets the bar for the challenge tier. Proportionality note: the most precisely-read source underwrites a two-hour tier that is first to be cut on overrun; the entry would be stronger if it also constrained the committed tier. Washburn et al. (2016), ICSE Companion - appears only in the synthesis; used correctly as a negative finding (no communication category among 155 postmortems) supporting the look-in-artefacts move. Not one of the counted entries and does not need to be. Overall: six-plus distinct, high-quality, peer-reviewed sources including academic research articles; no same-author or overlapping pairs; every entry states what was specifically learnt (my usual complaint - 'this source taught me a lot about X' - does not apply anywhere here). SENTENCES I HAD TO READ TWICE. 1. 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it: my evaluation scores each report against the team's history, not its tickets.' (no antecedent for 'That remedy'). 2. 'Deliverable 1 tests that transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise.' ('that transfer' reaches back two sentences). 3. 'The six do three jobs.' (seven sources have been presented). 4. 'The prototype classifies files only; the committed tier (the version I commit to delivering) adds object naming (Figure 3), with the AssetDatabase resolving identifiers to asset and script names.' 5. 'Across four SS3D weeks, between 46% and 100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text (23 of 26 in the week shown). The 60% target sits above the worst week.' (the reader must hold three numbers and do the comparison). 6. 'Week difficulty is then a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported beside the differences.' 7. 'It can falsify naming and activity claims, not file counts.' ('It' is the fidelity check, two sentences back). 8. 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough, nor does my own team's: its sprint pages were written up after the fact for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A).' 9. 'Measure: every need classified against a named artefact, with three needs where I name the artefact I rejected and why.' 10. 'Seven existing tools each cover one part of this (Appendix A): they summarise tickets and commits for engineers, take manual entry from game teams, or show asset history to developers and artists.' Ten re-reads in 2,461 words is the density signature the A1 marker punished; none of them is an error, which is why the student will not find them by proofreading. MECHANICAL TRAP CHECK. Template instruction text: none found - the rendered PDF (11 pages) carries only the student's own headings (Introduction, Literature Review, Project Proposal with Learning Goals / Scoping Evidence / Deliverables, References, Statement on Generative AI use, Appendices A-C). Cover fields: Name present, Topic Category present ('Developer / production tools'), Student ID is the placeholder '[STUDENT ID]' - flagged once here as instructed and marked as if filled. No table of contents is present in the rendered document; if the template supplies one, its field needs updating before submission - worth a 30-second check. Hours: the Deliverables table sums to 65 (12+16+4+3+15+7+4+2+2) with in-prac summing to 15 (2+5+1+1+4+1+1+0+0) - both correct, and the 50-outside-plus-15-in-prac split is stated in the lead sentence. Figures: three, numbered 1-3, each captioned and each cited in the body text; Figure 1 renders legibly with a source note ('Computed 17-18 Sep 2026 from git log --name-status'), Figure 2 is a real docked-Editor capture at readable resolution, Figure 3 is annotated and legible. Word count: body 2,461 (plus 27 on the cover), under the 2,500 limit excluding references; GenAI statement and Appendices A-C sit after the references and are uncounted. GenAI statement: present, dated, names the tool and the tasks, and - unusually and to the student's credit - names five AI-introduced errors that were caught and corrected, with evidence pointed at GENAI-EVIDENCE.md. That is the right way to declare it. The bracketed '[CONFIRM BEFORE SUBMISSION...]' line immediately after it must be deleted. References: 17 entries, APA-consistent, DOIs on every peer-reviewed item, retrieval dates on the n.d. web sources. Cross-check run both ways - every in-text citation (Anderson and Krathwohl, Bertram, Dourish and Bellotti, Endsley, Ko, Maddila, Nielsen, Nielsen and Molich, Pascarella, Stray, Washburn, Whitson) appears in the list, and every list entry is cited at least once, with McShaffry, ZeroStandup, Linear, HacknPlan, Perforce, Unity Technologies and Anchorpoint cited in Appendix A. No orphans either direction. Endsley (1995) is correctly cited as Human Factors 37(1), 32-64. CONTRADICTIONS FOUND. (a) 'The six do three jobs' versus seven presented entries. (b) Introduction asserts 'eight student producers read two versions' while Scoping Evidence makes eight a target with a floor of five. (c) Synthesis promises three explanations and adjudicates two - Stray's audience mechanism is raised and then dropped. (d) The floor design (five readers, five think-alouds) is a different design from the target (eight readers, six think-alouds) and the ordering of arms under it is unspecified. (e) Figure 2 shows a producer-facing artefact containing engine-internal categories ('Meta', 'DataConfig'), which sits against the Stray-derived claim that both reports are addressed to the producer. (f) Minor and explained, not a fault: Figure 1 reports SS3D at 17.5% over full history while Figure 2 and Appendix B report 24% for the sampled week - Appendix A states the different bases. MARK ARITHMETIC. 0.45 x 78 + 0.40 x 79 + 0.15 x 72 = 35.10 + 31.60 + 10.80 = 77.50. Rounded down to 77 per the instruction to report the lower value when torn, and because this student's AI mock marks have historically run high against the real marker. My honest expectation for the real mark is 74-78: the substance is solid D, and the density is the thing most likely to pull it lower with a marker who has 40 of these to read.

corrections.reason: The literature review names seven studies with their own paragraphs (the three explanations — Dourish & Bellotti, Whitson, Stray — plus the four further studies — Bertram, Ko, Pascarella, Maddila); the synthesis sentence and the count that follows it name only six, omitting Stray.

corrections.corrected: Dourish and Bellotti, with Whitson and Stray, explain why.
